title: Telling what happened
job: A four-sentence account in the past
verifiedBy: LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: THE PERFEKT IS THE SPOKEN PAST for nearly every verb: haben or sein in position two, the participle at the very END, which is M1's bracket for the fourth time. AND sein, haben and the modals prefer the PRÄTERITUM: war, hatte, konnte, wollte. That split is exactly why L1-M5 shipped war, waren, hatte and hatten and no participle for either — a course teaching ich bin gewesen as the everyday past would be teaching a form Germans rarely say.

THE AUXILIARY LAW: sein goes with MOVEMENT and CHANGE OF STATE — gegangen, gefahren, gekommen, geblieben, aufgestanden (L1-M4 shipped that last one) — and haben takes everything else. geblieben is the one worth naming, because staying is not movement and takes sein anyway; German counts it as a change of where you are.

AND THE RELIEF, because three courses in this repo say the opposite: THE GERMAN PARTICIPLE NEVER AGREES WITH ANYTHING. en-es, en-fr and en-it all make their participle agree in one auxiliary or the other; German simply does not. A learner arriving from any Romance language should be told so out loud, because they will otherwise spend weeks looking for a rule that is not there.

Participle formation is regular enough to state. WEAK: ge- plus the stem plus -t — gemacht, gearbeitet, gesagt. STRONG: ge- plus a often-changed stem plus -en — gegangen, gegessen, getrunken, gesehen. SEPARABLE: the ge- goes INSIDE — angerufen, eingestiegen, aufgestanden. That last shape is the one place a separable verb appears in this level without a modal in front of it, and it is still one clean token, so M4's ruling holds.

Each item here is an ACCOUNT of three or four short sentences, not one long one, and nearly every word in it has already been met. The honest new spend is the sequencers — zuerst, danach, schließlich, beside L1-M10's dann and also — and the participles an account needs. The Plusquamperfekt, Konjunktiv II beyond M1's frozen könnten, the passive and reported speech all stay OUT and belong to L3.

sentences.display: Zuerst habe ich gearbeitet. Dann bin ich nach Hause gegangen
sentences.cue: First I worked. Then I went home
sentences.literal: First have I worked. Then am I to house gone

words.note: The opener of an account, and fronting it pushes the subject behind the verb exactly as M6's day did. L1-M10's dann and this word are the two ends of a short story.
The auxiliary holds second place and the participle waits at the end. Front anything at all and the subject moves behind it — and the auxiliary is whichever of haben and sein the verb takes.

sentences.trap: Two auxiliaries in two sentences, and the verb decides which: arbeiten takes haben, gehen takes sein because it is movement. There is no choosing and no drift between them.
sentences.sound: tsoo-AIRST HAH-buh ikh guh-AR-buy-tet. dan bin ikh nakh HOW-zuh guh-GANG-en.

variations.display: Zuerst habe ich gegessen. Dann bin ich gegangen
variations.cue: First I ate. Then I left

variations.changed: no fronting, so the subject stays in front

variations.display: Zuerst bin ich nach Hause gegangen

mistake.why: The auxiliary holds second place: Zuerst habe ich gearbeitet.

sentences.usage: Opening an account of a day, an evening, a journey.

sentences.display: Es war spät. Also bin ich nach Hause gefahren
sentences.cue: It was late. So I drove home
sentences.literal: It was late. So am I to house driven

words.note: L1-M6's fahren as a strong participle — ge- plus the stem plus -en, and the vowel does not change here. Movement, so it takes sein.

sentences.trap: war and not ist gewesen. sein prefers the Präteritum in speech, which is why L1-M5 taught war and no participle for it at all — the everyday German past of "to be" is one word.
sentences.sound: es var shpayt. AL-zo bin ikh nakh HOW-zuh guh-FAH-ren. spät has a long ay.

variations.display: Es war spät. Also bin ich gegangen
variations.cue: It was late. So I left

variations.display: Es war kalt. Also bin ich nach Hause gefahren
variations.cue: It was cold. So I drove home

mistake.display: Es ist spät gewesen. Also bin ich nach Hause gefahren
mistake.why: sein prefers the Präteritum: Es war spät.

sentences.usage: The middle of an account, where a state explains a move.
sentences.mnemonic: sein and haben stay in the Präteritum. Everything else goes Perfekt.

sentences.display: Danach habe ich Frau Weber angerufen
sentences.cue: After that I called Ms Weber
sentences.literal: After-that have I Mrs Weber up-called

words.note: A step later in the same account, and it is heavier than dann — danach marks a real gap where dann is only the next thing.
M4's anrufen with the ge- INSIDE it: an + ge + rufen. Every separable verb builds its participle this way, and the result is still one token.

sentences.trap: The ge- goes in the MIDDLE of a separable verb and nowhere else. geanrufen is the form an English speaker builds by rule, and it does not exist.
sentences.sound: dah-NAKH HAH-buh ikh frow VAY-ber AN-guh-roo-fen. The stress of angerufen is on the AN.

variations.changed: a pronoun instead of a name

variations.display: Dann habe ich Frau Weber angerufen

variations.changed: another separable verb, and this one takes sein

mistake.display: Danach habe ich Frau Weber geanrufen
mistake.why: The ge- goes inside: Danach habe ich Frau Weber angerufen.

sentences.usage: Moving an account along one step.

sentences.display: Ich bin zu Hause geblieben. Es war sehr kalt
sentences.cue: I stayed at home. It was very cold
sentences.literal: I am at house stayed. It was very cold

words.note: Staying is not movement and it takes sein anyway. German counts it as a change of WHERE YOU ARE, which is the honest way to remember the whole sein list.

sentences.trap: bleiben takes sein even though nothing moved. Learn the auxiliary with the verb rather than from the meaning — the meaning gets this one wrong.
sentences.sound: ikh bin tsoo HOW-zuh guh-BLEE-ben. es var zair kalt.

variations.changed: M6's wir, with the plural auxiliary

variations.display: Es war kalt. Also bin ich zu Hause geblieben
variations.cue: It was cold. So I stayed at home

mistake.why: bleiben takes sein: Ich bin zu Hause geblieben.

sentences.usage: Explaining why an evening did not happen.
sentences.mnemonic: Staying counts as movement. Learn it with the verb.

sentences.display: Schließlich habe ich das Buch gelesen
sentences.literal: Finally have I the book read

words.note: The closer of an account. It carries a small sense of at last, which is why it is not simply the fourth dann.
A strong participle whose stem does not change: ge- plus les plus -en. Reading is not movement, so it takes haben.

sentences.trap: schließlich has TWO l's and an ß, and it is the longest word in the level. Writing schliesslich gives the index a key no row owns, exactly as M3 warned about Strasse.
sentences.sound: SHLEES-likh HAH-buh ikh das BOOKH guh-LAY-zen. The ß is a sharp s.

variations.display: Schließlich bin ich nach Hause gegangen
Ich habe schließlich das Buch gelesen
variations.cue: I read the book in the end

mistake.display: Schliesslich habe ich das Buch gelesen
mistake.why: The ß is never respelled: Schließlich habe ich das Buch gelesen.

sentences.usage: Closing an account — the last thing that happened.
sentences.mnemonic: schließlich ends it. And it keeps its ß.

sentences.display: Ich habe den Zug gesehen. Dann bin ich eingestiegen
sentences.cue: I saw the train. Then I got on
sentences.literal: I have the train seen. Then am I in-climbed

words.note: M3's sehen as a strong participle, and the stem does not change. Seeing is not movement, so it takes haben.
M4's einsteigen with the ge- inside and the stem vowel changed: ein + ge + stiegen. Boarding is movement, so it takes sein.

sentences.trap: Two participles, two auxiliaries, one sentence apart. sehen takes haben and einsteigen takes sein, and nothing about their shapes says so — only what they mean.
sentences.sound: ikh HAH-buh dayn tsook guh-ZAY-en. dan bin ikh INE-guh-shtee-gen.

variations.display: Dann bin ich in den Zug eingestiegen
variations.cue: Then I got on the train
variations.changed: naming the train, with M4's accusative of motion
a person instead of a thing

mistake.why: Boarding is movement: Dann bin ich eingestiegen.

sentences.usage: The middle of a journey told afterwards.
sentences.mnemonic: Meaning picks the auxiliary. Shape tells you nothing.

sentences.display: Sie ist gekommen. Wir haben zusammen gegessen
sentences.literal: She is come. We have together eaten

words.note: L1-M1's kommen as a strong participle, with the vowel back to o. Coming is movement, so it takes sein — and the participle does not change for sie.

sentences.trap: THE PARTICIPLE DOES NOT AGREE. Spanish, French and Italian would all change something here for a feminine subject; German changes nothing at all, ever, in either auxiliary. M5's zusammen is doing its plain adverb job beside it.
sentences.sound: zee ist guh-KOM-men. veer HAH-ben tsoo-ZAM-men guh-GESS-en.

variations.changed: a masculine subject, and the participle is identical
the plural reading of sie, decided by the verb

mistake.why: The German participle never agrees: Sie ist gekommen.

sentences.usage: Telling somebody how an evening went.

sentences.display: Ich konnte nicht kommen. Ich hatte keine Zeit
sentences.cue: I couldn't come. I had no time
sentences.literal: I could not come. I had no time

words.note: M1's können in the Präteritum, because the modals stay there in speech just as sein and haben do. Ich habe nicht kommen können exists and is rare.

sentences.trap: The modals do NOT go into the Perfekt in ordinary speech. konnte, wollte, musste are what people say, and a learner building ich habe gekonnt is technically producing German that nobody uses.
sentences.sound: ikh KON-tuh nikht KOM-men. ikh HAT-tuh KY-nuh tsite.

variations.changed: the reason on its own, with M8's kein

mistake.why: A modal stays in the Präteritum: Ich konnte nicht kommen.

sentences.usage: Apologising afterwards for not turning up.
sentences.mnemonic: Modals stay behind. konnte, wollte, musste.

sentences.display: Er hat gesagt, dass er kommt
sentences.literal: He has said, that he comes

words.note: A weak participle — ge- plus sag plus -t. What he actually said is passed on with the words themselves; changing them is L3's business.

sentences.trap: L1-M9's dass sends its verb to the END of its own clause, exactly as weil does, and the comma in front of it is not optional. German commas are grammar rather than breathing, which is the opposite of the English habit.
sentences.sound: air hat guh-ZAHKT, das air komt. dass has a short a and a sharp s.

variations.display: Sie hat gesagt, dass sie kommt
Er hat gesagt, dass er keine Zeit hat
variations.cue: He said he has no time
variations.changed: a longer clause, verb still at the end

mistake.display: Er hat gesagt dass er kommt
mistake.why: dass takes a comma in front: Er hat gesagt, dass er kommt.

sentences.usage: Passing a message on — M7's call, told afterwards.
sentences.mnemonic: dass sends the verb away. And it brings a comma.

sentences.display: Zuerst war es kalt. Dann habe ich Tee getrunken. Schließlich war mir wärmer
sentences.cue: First it was cold. Then I drank tea. In the end I was warmer
sentences.literal: First was it cold. Then have I tea drunk. Finally was to-me warmer

words.note: L1-M9's warm with M9's umlaut comparative, inside M8's subjectless family: Mir war wärmer, with war second and no subject anywhere.

sentences.trap: Three sentences, three fronted words, and the verb second in every one of them. That is the whole architecture of a German account, and it is visible here in one line.
sentences.sound: tsoo-AIRST var es kalt. dan HAH-buh ikh tay guh-TROONK-en. SHLEES-likh var meer VAIR-mer.

variations.display: Zuerst war es kalt. Dann habe ich Tee getrunken
variations.cue: First it was cold. Then I drank tea
In the end I was warmer
variations.changed: the close on its own, still with no subject

variations.display: Zuerst war es kalt. Schließlich war mir wärmer
variations.cue: First it was cold. In the end I was warmer
variations.changed: the two states, with the step between them left out

mistake.why: The verb holds second place: Schließlich war mir wärmer.

sentences.usage: A whole small story, told the way German tells one.
sentences.mnemonic: Front what you like. The verb still comes second.
